How a project works · Relevant experience

The infrastructure behind your plant network

Operational technology (OT) monitors and controls physical equipment. Its network needs to suit the distances, conditions, and maintenance demands of your plant, as well as the devices it connects.

Site Assessments and Network Planning

Map the existing connections and plan for equipment additions or upgrades. Review distances, traffic needs, spare capacity, and exposure to heat, dust, moisture, vibration, and electrical noise.

Industrial Switches and Equipment Connections

Install and configure network equipment connecting machine controllers (PLCs), operator screens (HMIs), and plant systems. Plan how production areas connect to the wider plant network.

Copper and Fiber Connections

Review cable types, routes, patching, and connections between equipment and production areas. Match the network links to the distance, environment, and equipment requirements.

Network Cabinets and Cable Organization

Plan equipment placement, patch panels, cable routing, and labels. Keep connections identifiable and accessible, with room for maintenance and planned expansion.

Traffic Separation and Redundant Paths

Configure network traffic separation and support Parallel Redundancy Protocol (PRP) networks with two communication paths. Agree on the required connections and failure checks with your team.

Troubleshooting, Testing, and Handover

Investigate unreliable connections and check the agreed changes. Record the results and update network drawings, equipment lists, and connection records so your team can support the installation.

What to include in your inquiry

  • The affected equipment and the symptoms or planned change
  • Your site location and preferred timing
  • Whether production is affected and any available maintenance window
  • The IT, maintenance, and equipment-vendor contacts involved

A high-level description is enough to begin. We agree on how to exchange technical records after discussing the project.

A handover your team can use

An assessment gives you findings and recommended next steps. For installation or upgrades, the agreed handover can include drawings of the installed connections, cabinet layouts, cable and port records, and test results. We identify what was verified, what changed, and anything still needing attention.

BEFORE WORK STARTS

Plan around the equipment and the people who run it.

Coordinate

Agree on authorized changes, site requirements, work windows, and the roles of your IT team, maintenance staff, and equipment vendors.

Test

Define the checks needed to confirm the result, who reviews them, and when production can resume after any agreed interruption.

Prepare for recovery

Identify the records, configurations, and vendor support needed to restore the previous setup if a change does not pass its checks.

Common Questions

Can you work on an existing plant network?

Yes. We start with the installed equipment, available records, and the change you need. The plan identifies what can remain, what needs updating, and how the work fits around production and your existing support teams.

What is a plant network backbone?

It is the main set of network links connecting production areas and plant systems. Individual machines connect through local switches, which connect back to this wider network.

Does this include programming our machines?

This page covers industrial network connectivity. Changes to control programs, machine behavior, or electrical systems are not implied by a network project and require separate scope and appropriate expertise.

Can you guarantee there will be no downtime?

No. We discuss interruption risks and agree on work windows, testing, and recovery arrangements before changes. The requirements depend on your equipment and the proposed work.

Can we bring in our existing IT provider or machine vendor?

Yes. Identify those contacts during planning so responsibilities, approvals, and any vendor-dependent work can be agreed.
